summary: A report on an experiment in which Rand graphic consoles were connected over the ARPANET to UCSB's Online System. The first phase let visitors from UCSB and TRW use it from Rand, and the second phase involved cleaning up the implementation and revisiting strategy.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC reports on an experiment using Rand graphics consoles to access UCSB's On-Line System over the network. The first phase had succeeded, and the team was improving the initial implementation.

subtitle: A progress report on using UCSB's On-Line System from Rand graphics consoles.

tldr.problem: The Network Graphics Meeting outlined experiments to explore graphics over the network.
tldr.mechanism: Rand consoles used a module in the Rand Network Services Program to access UCSB's On-Line System, with input from a tablet and on-screen function areas.
tldr.outcome: The first phase was completed in August, while the second phase was still refining the implementation and strategy. The unit metadata says it updates RFC 74.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 225 as Unknown and says it updates RFC 74. It records a 1971 graphics experiment and its planned follow-up.

sections.title: The Experiment and Its Progress
sections.content:
One experiment outlined at the July Network Graphics Meeting was to use the UCSB On-Line System (OLS) from graphics consoles at Rand. The connection was completed in the latter half of August, and users from UCSB and TRW had accessed OLS from Rand consoles.

The RFC says this completed the first phase. The second phase involved cleaning up the implementation and reviewing and modifying the initial strategies.
sections.plainLanguage: Users at Rand had connected to the UCSB system and used it from graphics consoles. The team was still improving the first version.

sections.title: Network Interface and Console
sections.content:
The UCSB OLS interface described in RFC 74 was modified to conform to current NCP and ICP protocols and to a general graphics description. OLS receives an EBCDIC-like input byte stream and generates an unstructured graphical output stream.

Rand used its Video-Graphics System consoles, already connected through the Rand Network Services Program. An OLS module was added to that program.
sections.plainLanguage: UCSB updated its network interface, and Rand added an OLS option to its existing network program. This let the Rand consoles send input and receive graphics.

sections.title: Tablet Input and Display
sections.content:
A user moved a tablet cursor to a function button on the screen and pressed the tablet pen. The screen included a feedback line, an OLS output area and a lower sensitive area containing function buttons and character entry.

The rightmost column included CALL and CLOSE to connect or disconnect, plus COPY for hardcopy output through an SC 4060. Other areas contained OLS function buttons and controls for numbers, characters and punctuation. The figures show a login sequence and SIN and COS curves from -PI to +PI.
sections.plainLanguage: Users selected on-screen functions with a tablet pen. The display combined an output area with controls for connecting, entering characters and using OLS functions.

sections.title: Planned Follow-Up
sections.content:
The authors planned to present a description of the protocols and techniques, with conclusions, at the October graphics meeting. They also planned to show a film of the OLS experiment from Rand.

The RFC says the protocols would be documented when the experimentation was complete.
sections.plainLanguage: The group planned to present what it learned and show a film of the experiment. Detailed protocol documentation was expected after the experiment ended.

references.text: RFC 74, describing the UCSB OLS network interface.
